nodes.title: Strategy, business model, objectives and tactics

teaching_content.core_explanation: Strategy is a coherent set of longer-term choices about where an organisation will compete or operate, how it will create and capture value, what capabilities it will build and what it will deliberately not do. Objectives are intended results; tactics are specific actions used to implement choices; a business model explains how value is created, delivered and captured through customers, activities, resources, partners, revenues and costs. These concepts are connected but not interchangeable. 'Increase revenue by 10%' is an objective, not a strategy. 'Run a social-media campaign' is a tactic. A strategy would explain which customers the business chooses, what distinctive value it offers, what activities/capabilities support that position and how those choices fit together. Strategic consistency matters because functions can undermine each other: a premium differentiation strategy is weakened by low-service operations, indiscriminate discounting or underinvestment in quality. Strategy also develops through a mixture of deliberate planning and learning; new evidence can justify adaptation without implying that the original strategy was meaningless.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: This node provides the organising logic for higher-level Business judgement and prevents students from labelling any objective or action as 'strategy'.
definitions: strategy: coherent longer-term choices about where/how an organisation will create and capture value
objective: intended result
tactic: specific action used to implement a strategy
business model: mechanism by which the organisation creates, delivers and captures value
strategic consistency: degree to which choices and activities reinforce rather than contradict one another
important_boundaries: strategy is not a target
tactics are not strategy
business model is not the same as business plan
adaptation is not automatically strategic failure
facts: strategy allocates scarce resources and creates trade-offs
competitive position depends on activity fit as well as statements
implementation capability affects whether intended strategy becomes actual performance
mechanisms: clear choices -> aligned resources/activities -> differentiated or lower-cost value -> performance
contradictory functional choices -> weak fit -> cost/service/brand conflict
new evidence -> strategic learning -> adaptation
causal_relationships: purpose/objectives -> strategic choices -> functional plans -> capability/resource commitments -> outcomes
examples: A low-cost airline strategy involves aircraft utilisation, airport choices, service design, staffing, pricing and route economics working together; a cheap ticket alone is a tactic/outcome, not the strategy.
non_examples: Calling 'open three new stores' a complete strategy without explaining target market, economics and capability.
applications: explain how functional choices reinforce a position
real_world_transfer: Identify when a firm's stated strategy conflicts with its actual operating choices.
assumptions: Strategic intent is observable enough to compare with activities and outcomes.
limitations: Real strategies can be partly emergent; retrospective success stories can overstate deliberate planning.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: A strategy is a long-term objective.
misconceptions.correction: An objective states a desired result; strategy explains the coherent choices used to pursue it.

nodes.title: Competitive advantage

teaching_content.core_explanation: Competitive advantage exists when a business can create and capture superior value relative to alternatives through a cost position, differentiation, focus, distinctive capability, asset, relationship, data, network, location, brand, intellectual property or combination of these. Advantage is not the same as being temporarily successful or having high market share. A useful analysis asks three questions: what specific mechanism creates the advantage; why does that mechanism matter to customer value or cost; and what prevents competitors from copying, substituting or neutralising it? A lower-cost position can come from scale, process, sourcing, technology or business-model design, while differentiation can come from quality, convenience, brand, innovation, service or other valued attributes. Sustainable advantage is difficult because competitors learn, technology changes and customer preferences move. Capabilities often depend on systems and relationships that take time to build, making them harder to imitate than isolated product features.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Competitive advantage links strategy to observable mechanisms rather than vague claims that a company is 'better than competitors'.
definitions: competitive advantage: ability to create/capture superior value relative to rivals in a way competitors cannot immediately neutralise
cost advantage: structurally lower relevant cost for comparable value
differentiation advantage: valued distinction supporting preference or reduced price sensitivity
capability: coordinated ability to perform an activity reliably
important_boundaries: market leadership is not proof of durable advantage
a feature can be copied and therefore may not be an enduring advantage
low price is not the same as low cost
brand awareness is not automatically advantage
facts: advantages can erode
activity systems can be harder to copy than single features
trade-offs can protect a distinctive position
mechanisms: lower process/input cost -> lower price or higher margin -> competitive effect
distinctive benefit -> preference/lower substitutability -> demand/pricing power
learning/network/data -> cumulative capability -> imitation barrier
causal_relationships: capability/resource -> customer/cost benefit -> relative performance -> reinvestment/learning -> potential reinforcement
examples: A logistics company may have advantage not because it owns trucks, but because route density, data, hubs and process reliability combine to lower unit delivery cost and improve service.
non_examples: Calling a one-off viral campaign a sustainable competitive advantage.
applications: connect advantage to customer or cost economics
real_world_transfer: Challenge a claim of competitive advantage by asking what prevents rivals copying it.
assumptions: Relevant competitors and customer alternatives are identified correctly.
limitations: Advantage can be multi-causal and hard to measure; industry disruption can invalidate previously durable strengths.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: A company with the largest market share has competitive advantage.
misconceptions.correction: Share may result from many causes and can be temporary; advantage requires a value/cost mechanism with some defensibility.

interpretation: market share/margins can support but do not prove advantage

models_frameworks: Porter's generic-strategy concepts may be course-specific analytical frameworks rather than the definition of advantage

nodes.title: SWOT, PESTLE and strategic environmental analysis

teaching_content.core_explanation: PESTLE and SWOT are structuring tools, not sources of strategy. PESTLE groups external influences into political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental categories. Its value lies in prompting broad scanning and then tracing specific effects through the business. SWOT summarises internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats. The categories are not self-explanatory: 'AI = opportunity' or 'inflation = threat' is too shallow. The analyst must identify the exposure, mechanism, scale, timing and likely response. The same external change can be an opportunity for one business and a threat to another. SWOT is most useful as synthesis after evidence gathering, not as a brainstorming list that substitutes for analysis. A strength must be relative and relevant to the decision; an opportunity must be exploitable given the business's resources and capabilities. Good use links external evidence to internal capability and then to strategic choices.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: These are commonly taught models and therefore high-risk for mechanical exam use. The node teaches how to convert a list into causal analysis.
definitions: PESTLE: framework for scanning political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental influences
SWOT: framework summarising internal strengths/weaknesses and external opportunities/threats
strategic environmental analysis: evidence-based interpretation of external and internal conditions relevant to choices
important_boundaries: PESTLE factors overlap
SWOT categories are judgements not facts
a trend is not an opportunity until the business can exploit it
a strength matters only relative to objective/competitors/context
facts: external factors interact
internal capabilities shape exposure to external change
lists do not prioritise significance
mechanisms: external change -> business-specific transmission -> opportunity/threat
capability/resource -> ability to exploit/defend -> strategic option
causal_relationships: environment + capability -> strategic issue -> options -> choice
examples: Higher energy prices may be a cost threat for an energy-intensive manufacturer but strengthen demand for an energy-efficiency technology provider.
non_examples: Writing 'technology: AI' in PESTLE with no explanation of what changes for the business.
real_world_transfer: Reject a SWOT that labels a firm's large size as a strength without showing how size creates a relevant benefit.
assumptions: Categories help organise evidence but do not determine materiality.
limitations: Frameworks can encourage static lists, duplicate factors and subjective labelling; they do not predict the future.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Completing a SWOT is strategic analysis.
misconceptions.correction: SWOT is a summary structure; analysis requires evidence, mechanisms, prioritisation and implications.

teaching_content.core_explanation: The Ansoff product-market framework classifies growth direction according to whether products and markets are existing or new to the business. Market penetration seeks more activity with existing products in existing markets; market development takes existing products to new markets; product development introduces new products to existing markets; diversification combines new products and new markets. The framework is useful because increasing newness generally changes information and capability requirements, but it should not be taught as a deterministic risk ladder. 'New' is a continuum: entering an adjacent geography with known customers may be less uncertain than attempting penetration in a collapsing home market. Diversification can be related or unrelated, and risk depends on capabilities, finance, competitive response and the quality of evidence. The framework organises strategic direction; it does not tell managers whether organic growth, acquisition, licensing or another method should be used.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: It gives learners a structured way to distinguish growth direction from growth method while requiring contextual risk analysis.
definitions: market penetration: existing product/existing market growth
market development: existing product/new market
product development: new product/existing market
diversification: new product/new market
important_boundaries: growth direction is not growth method
newness is not binary in reality
diversification is not automatically the riskiest option in every context
framework does not assess financial viability
facts: different directions require different knowledge/capabilities
market/product newness can increase uncertainty
related diversification can share capabilities
mechanisms: greater unfamiliarity -> higher information/capability gap -> implementation risk
shared resources/capabilities -> reduced expansion cost/risk
causal_relationships: growth direction -> capability/market requirements -> finance/operations/marketing implications
examples: A UK coffee chain opening in France with the same offer is market development; launching packaged coffee into its existing UK customer base is product development.
non_examples: Calling acquisition 'diversification' merely because it is an external growth method.
real_world_transfer: Explain why adjacent market development can be safer than aggressive penetration in a declining market.
assumptions: Existing/new categories are defined from the focal firm's perspective.
limitations: The matrix says little about competitive advantage, execution, finance or degree of relatedness.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Diversification is always the riskiest strategy.
misconceptions.correction: It typically adds unfamiliarity, but actual risk depends on adjacency, capability, market conditions and implementation.

nodes.title: Porter's Five Forces and industry structure

teaching_content.core_explanation: Porter's Five Forces is an industry-structure framework examining rivalry among existing competitors, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of suppliers and bargaining power of buyers. Its purpose is to understand structural pressures that influence how economic value is divided among participants and how attractive or defensible a position may be. Rivalry is shaped by factors such as number/balance of competitors, growth and exit barriers. Entry threat depends on barriers such as scale, capital, regulation, brand, access and switching costs. Substitutes are different solutions to the same customer need, not merely direct rivals. Supplier and buyer power depend on concentration, alternatives, switching costs, information and importance. The framework should be applied through mechanisms, not by rating each force 'high/low' without evidence. It also has limits: industry boundaries can be fuzzy, complements and ecosystems matter, and digital/platform change can alter structure quickly.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Five Forces helps learners analyse competition beyond simple rival counts and connects industry structure to pricing, cost and bargaining power.
definitions: rivalry: competitive pressure among existing firms
entry threat: pressure from potential new competitors
substitute: alternative solution satisfying similar customer need
supplier power: supplier ability to capture value/influence terms
buyer power: customer ability to influence price/terms
important_boundaries: substitute is not the same as direct competitor
force strength is evidence-based, not inherent
framework analyses industry structure, not company resources directly
high rivalry does not automatically mean no profitable niche exists
facts: switching costs affect power
concentration and alternatives affect bargaining
entry barriers can erode
mechanisms: strong buyer power -> price/service pressure -> margin
strong supplier power -> input cost/terms -> margin/risk
substitute availability -> price ceiling/demand elasticity
examples: Rail travel faces substitutes including cars, coaches and video conferencing for some journeys; substitutes need not sell the same product.
non_examples: Listing five forces without explaining why each changes business economics.
real_world_transfer: Recognise that a dominant supplier can be strategically important even when final-market rivalry is weak.
assumptions: Industry boundary and customer need are defined sensibly.
limitations: Static snapshot; underplays firm-specific capability, complements, networks and rapid ecosystem change.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: A substitute is another brand in the same market.
misconceptions.correction: A substitute can be a different solution that satisfies the same underlying need.

nodes.title: BCG growth-share matrix and portfolio logic
nodes.recommended_depth: A-level where course requires; reusable analytical framework

teaching_content.core_explanation: The BCG growth-share matrix is a portfolio framework that classifies business units or products by market growth and relative market share into stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs/pets. The historical logic is that high-growth markets often require investment while high relative share may support cost/competitive strength and cash generation. It can prompt useful resource-allocation questions—where should cash be invested, harvested or challenged?—but it should not dictate decisions. High share does not guarantee profit or cash; low share can coexist with a profitable niche or strategic complement; market growth can be measured poorly; and synergies across portfolio units can matter. Relative market share also requires a defined competitor denominator. The matrix is therefore a teaching simplification, not a law of product performance.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: The model is widely taught and useful when its assumptions are explicit, making it a strong case study in separating framework from fact.
definitions: star: high growth/high relative share category
cash cow: low growth/high relative share
question mark: high growth/low relative share
dog/pet: low growth/low relative share
relative market share: focal share relative to a defined leading competitor under the chosen convention
important_boundaries: category does not determine action
market share does not guarantee profitability
growth does not equal attractiveness
portfolio synergies can override stand-alone category logic
facts: matrix uses only two dimensions
classification depends on market definition and thresholds
cash needs and generation are hypotheses rather than automatic truths
mechanisms: growth -> potential investment requirement
share/scale -> possible cost/cash effect
portfolio cash flows -> resource-allocation choice
causal_relationships: market dynamics + relative position -> resource needs/cash potential -> portfolio decision
examples: A low-share specialist B2B unit can be highly profitable and strategically important despite appearing as a 'dog' under a simplistic matrix.
applications: evaluate portfolio decisions beyond the matrix
real_world_transfer: Challenge a divestment recommendation based only on a BCG quadrant.
assumptions: Market growth/share meaningfully relate to investment need and competitive position.
limitations: Two dimensions omit profitability, synergy, capability, cash timing and disruption.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Cash cows always generate lots of cash and dogs should be sold.
misconceptions.correction: Those are model implications based on assumptions; actual economics and strategic role must be tested.

methods: market growth/share calculations from BUS-MKT-002; relative-share convention course-specific
interpretation: inputs are estimates; quadrant is not an instruction

nodes.confidence: high as framework description; lower as decision rule
uncertainties: Exact relative-share calculation conventions vary by teaching context.

nodes.title: Organic growth, mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures and alliances

teaching_content.core_explanation: Growth direction and growth method are separate decisions. Organic growth develops sales, assets and capabilities internally. Mergers and acquisitions combine or transfer ownership/control of existing organisations. Joint ventures create jointly controlled activity for a specific purpose, while strategic alliances enable cooperation without full ownership combination. External growth can accelerate access to customers, assets, technology or capabilities, but speed comes with valuation, financing, integration, culture and execution risk. Claimed synergies should be treated as hypotheses: cost synergy requires an identifiable overlap or scale mechanism; revenue synergy requires evidence that combined products, channels or customers actually increase revenue. Acquisition premiums and debt can destroy value if expected benefits fail. Organic growth is slower but can preserve culture/control and allow learning. The right method depends on urgency, capability availability, finance, uncertainty, integration difficulty and strategic fit.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Growth method is a major whole-business decision involving finance, people, operations and strategy rather than a generic list of advantages and disadvantages.
definitions: organic growth: internal expansion of activity/capability
merger: combination of organisations under agreed ownership/control structure
acquisition/takeover: one organisation obtains control of another
joint venture: separately governed activity owned/controlled jointly by partners
strategic alliance: cooperation between independent organisations without full ownership combination
synergy: benefit from combination exceeding stand-alone outcomes
important_boundaries: acquisition is a method, not an Ansoff direction
synergy is not automatic
speed is not necessarily value
joint venture does not remove partner conflict
facts: acquisitions require financing and integration
culture/process differences can block expected synergies
alliances can provide access while limiting capital commitment
mechanisms: acquisition -> immediate assets/customers -> integration -> realised or failed synergy
organic growth -> staged investment/learning -> slower scale
joint venture -> shared resource/risk -> governance complexity
examples: Buying a competitor for distribution access may save years of organic build, but only if systems and customer relationships transfer successfully and the purchase price is justified.
non_examples: Counting duplicated headquarters roles as guaranteed synergy before implementation.
real_world_transfer: Question whether an acquisition's claimed synergies are specific, measurable and realistically implementable.
assumptions: Target information and synergy estimates are sufficiently reliable.
limitations: Post-deal performance is hard to attribute; integration costs and cultural effects are uncertain.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: External growth is better because it is faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speed can be valuable but acquisition price, integration, debt and culture can make external growth more risky or value-destroying.

interpretation: synergy estimates should be linked to specific cost/revenue mechanisms and timing

nodes.title: Innovation, R&D, intellectual property, digital transformation and disruptive technology

teaching_content.core_explanation: Innovation is implemented change that creates or is intended to create value. It can involve products, services, processes, business models, marketing or organisation. Research and development (R&D) is one route to generating knowledge and technical possibilities but is not synonymous with innovation: inventions that are never implemented create no business value, while process innovations can arise without formal R&D. Intellectual property (IP) includes legal and practical mechanisms that help protect knowledge, brands, inventions or creative outputs, though protection varies by type and jurisdiction. Digital transformation is not simply buying software; it involves redesigning processes, skills, data, customer interactions and decision systems so technology changes how value is created or delivered. Artificial intelligence is best treated within this broader capability logic: AI can automate or augment tasks, personalise services, analyse data or create new products, but value depends on data quality, process redesign, skills, governance, customer trust, cost and risk. 'Disruptive' technology should not be used as a synonym for new technology; disruption describes significant changes in competitive or business-model conditions, not novelty alone.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Technology is a current board emphasis, but the underlying subject truth is capability and value creation rather than memorising fashionable tools.
definitions: innovation: implemented change intended to create value
R&D: systematic work to increase knowledge/develop new applications
intellectual property: legally or commercially protectable knowledge/creative asset rights
digital transformation: organisational change using digital technology to redesign value creation/delivery
AI: computational systems performing tasks such as prediction/generation/classification that can augment or automate business activity
important_boundaries: R&D is not innovation
technology purchase is not transformation
AI adoption is not automatically productivity
new technology is not automatically disruptive
IP protection does not guarantee commercial advantage
facts: technology adoption requires complementary skills/processes
innovation creates uncertainty and option value
digital systems can increase data dependency/security/privacy risk
mechanisms: technology + process redesign + capability -> productivity/customer/quality effect
innovation -> differentiation/cost/business-model change -> competitive response
AI -> task automation/augmentation -> job redesign -> training/control changes
causal_relationships: technology investment -> adoption/capability -> actual use -> business outcome
examples: A firm deploying generative AI for customer support gains value only if knowledge sources are accurate, escalation rules work, staff can supervise outputs and customer trust is maintained.
non_examples: Calling a software purchase digital transformation before workflows or outcomes change.
real_world_transfer: Explain why the same AI tool can raise productivity in one business and create costly errors in another.
assumptions: Technology performance is evaluated in the actual process/customer context rather than vendor claims.
limitations: Technology changes quickly; current examples age faster than the underlying concepts; legal/ethical requirements evolve.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: AI creates a separate new Business topic.
misconceptions.correction: AI is a current technology application whose business consequences are understood through innovation, capability, data, people, process, risk and customer concepts.

interpretation: technology ROI/productivity claims require causal and baseline evidence
common_errors: attributing all post-adoption improvement to technology

nodes.title: Organisational change, resistance and implementation

teaching_content.core_explanation: Organisational change moves a business from current ways of working toward a different state. Change can be incremental or transformational, planned or emergent, and can involve strategy, structure, technology, process, people, culture or ownership. Resistance is not automatically irrational opposition. Employees may resist because they expect workload, skill loss, status change, job insecurity, poor implementation or because they hold information decision makers have missed. Effective implementation therefore requires more than communication: the organisation must align skills, processes, systems, incentives, leadership, resources and measures with the desired change. Participation can improve information and ownership, while urgent/high-risk situations may require faster directive action. Pilots and staged roll-outs can reduce downside and create learning where change is uncertain. Change can fail even when technology or formal structure is delivered if day-to-day behaviour does not change. Named models such as force-field analysis, Kotter-type staged models or change tactics should be treated as analytical aids rather than universal recipes.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Implementation is where strategy becomes actual performance and exposes the interdependence of people, systems, finance and operations.
definitions: organisational change: alteration of strategy, structure, process, technology, people or culture
resistance to change: behaviour or attitudes opposing/slowing change
change implementation: practical transition from intended change to embedded working behaviour
pilot: bounded trial used to test and learn before wider deployment
important_boundaries: resistance is not always irrational
communication is not implementation
installation is not adoption
planned models are not guarantees
facts: incentives and measures can reinforce old behaviour
capability gaps can block adoption
change has transition costs and productivity dips
mechanisms: clear case + participation/leadership -> understanding/commitment
training/process/incentive alignment -> behaviour adoption
pilot -> evidence -> adaptation -> reduced rollout risk
causal_relationships: strategy change -> process/skill/system requirements -> adoption -> outcome
misaligned incentives -> old behaviour -> change failure
examples: A CRM system goes live technically, but sales staff keep private spreadsheets because targets reward short-term sales and the new system adds admin. The technology is installed but the change is not implemented.
non_examples: Explaining every objection as fear of change without checking whether employees identified real risks.
real_world_transfer: Identify when a failed transformation is caused by incentives/processes rather than employee attitude.
assumptions: Desired state and success measures can be defined sufficiently.
limitations: Change is non-linear; political, emotional and emergent effects can make staged models simplistic.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: People resist change because they dislike change.
misconceptions.correction: Resistance can reflect rational concerns about risk, workload, capability, fairness, identity or flawed design.

methods: project/network analysis may support change planning through BUS-EVI-008

models_frameworks: course-specific change frameworks such as Kotter/Schlesinger should be separately mapped
uncertainties: Named change frameworks required vary by qualification.
